summary.title: Building a Vector Space Indexing Engine in Python
summary.one_liner: You learn how to build a simple search engine in Python by turning documents into word-count concordances and ranking them against a query with cosine-style vector space similarity.
keywords: why is it hard to build google
takeaways: A concordance is a per-document count of each word, which can serve as a simple vector.
Cosine-style similarity between a query concordance and a document concordance gives a 0 to 1 relevance score.
Sorting documents by that score produces ranked search results; the example ran on seven blog post intros.
Limitations: no boolean search, bias toward smaller documents, and high CPU cost that grows with document count (author tested up to 50,000 documents).
Scaling to web size needs sharding across machines, which the author links to Anna Patterson's essay on why search engines are hard.
summary.summary: The author builds a small search engine in Python from scratch, starting with a concordance function that counts each word in a document. A VectorCompare class computes magnitude and a normalized dot product between a query concordance and each document concordance, returning a score from 0 to 1. The example indexes seven blog post titles and opening paragraphs, then runs sample queries and prints ranked results. The post closes by discussing limitations: no boolean queries, bias toward small documents, and CPU cost, and it notes why web-scale indexing is much harder. The code is Python 2 (uses has_key, iteritems, raw_input).
